title: Design a Distributed Task Scheduler (like cron at scale) — job storage, scheduling (priority queue / time-based), at-least-once execution, deduplication, failure retry, multi-tenant isolation.
shortTitle: Design a Distributed Task Scheduler (like cron at scale)
topicTitle: Design a Distributed Task Scheduler (like cron at scale)

s1_definition.profdef: A distributed task scheduler reliably runs jobs at or after a specified time across a cluster of workers. It persists job definitions and schedules in durable storage, selects due jobs using a time-ordered or priority structure, guarantees at-least-once execution while deduplicating so a job is not run twice, retries failures with backoff, and isolates tenants so one customer's workload cannot starve another's. Correctness under worker crashes and clock skew is its central challenge.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India must run many timed jobs: calculate daily interest at midnight, send Rajesh his statement on the first of the month, retry a failed settlement in ten minutes. A single server running cron is fragile because if it dies, nothing runs. A distributed scheduler spreads these jobs across many servers, keeps a durable list of what must run and when, makes sure each job runs even if a worker crashes, avoids running the same interest calculation twice, and keeps one busy customer's jobs from blocking everyone else's.
s1_definition.oneliner: Persist jobs durably, pick due ones by time or priority, guarantee at-least-once with deduplication, retry with backoff, and isolate tenants.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A distributed task scheduler reliably runs jobs at or after a specified time across a cluster of workers. It persists job definitions and schedules in durable storage, selects due jobs using a time-ordered or priority structure, guarantees at-least-once execution while deduplicating so a job is not run twice, retries failures with backoff, and isolates tenants so one customer's workload cannot starve another's. Correctness under worker crashes and clock skew is its central challenge.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India must run many timed jobs: calculate daily interest at midnight, send Rajesh his statement on the first of the month, retry a failed settlement in ten minutes. A single server running cron is fragile because if it dies, nothing runs. A distributed scheduler spreads these jobs across many servers, keeps a durable list of what must run and when, makes sure each job runs even if a worker crashes, avoids running the same interest calculation twice, and keeps one busy customer's jobs from blocking everyone else's.

**One line to remember:** Persist jobs durably, pick due ones by time or priority, guarantee at-least-once with deduplication, retry with backoff, and isolate tenants.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India must calculate daily interest for every account at midnight, and the single cron server that used to do this crashed one night, so no interest was applied. The real problem is reliability across machines. This is exactly how durable job storage plus at-least-once execution across workers solves it.

Problem 2 — a worker picked up the interest job, calculated it, but crashed before reporting success, so the scheduler re-dispatched it and risked applying interest twice. The real problem is exactly-once effect under at-least-once delivery. This is exactly how deduplication by a stable execution id prevents double interest.

Problem 3 — one corporate tenant schedules thousands of report jobs at once, threatening to delay Rajesh's simple statement job. The real problem is fairness. This is exactly how multi-tenant isolation with per-tenant limits works.

We build a runnable scheduler core: a `JobStore`, a `Scheduler` that finds due jobs and claims them with leases, a `WorkerPool` that executes with retry and deduplication, and tenant caps. The demo schedules an interest job and several tenant report jobs, simulates a worker crash that triggers re-dispatch, shows deduplication preventing double execution, and shows a tenant cap.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a daily interest job for the bank tenant, four report jobs for a flooding corporate tenant, and Rajesh's statement job, all due now, with a per-tenant cap of two.

Step 1: The scheduler asks the store for due jobs and claims each with a lease, flipping it from pending to running so no two workers take the same job. Claimed jobs are submitted to the worker pool.

Step 2: The worker pool enforces the tenant cap. The first two corporate report jobs run, but the third and fourth find the corporate tenant at its cap of two concurrent and are deferred back to pending, protecting Rajesh's statement job and the interest job from being starved.

Step 3: The interest job executes, records its effect id, and completes. Then the demo simulates the interest worker crashing by expiring its lease, which returns the job to pending even though its effect was already applied.

Step 4: The scheduler re-dispatches the interest job. The worker sees the effect id already recorded, so deduplication skips re-applying interest and simply marks the job done. The data that changed is each job's state advancing, the per-tenant running counts rising and falling, and the executed-effects set recording completed work so repeats are harmless.

```
2026-11-01 00:00:00 [INFO] executing JOB-INTEREST (calc-interest) attempt 1
2026-11-01 00:00:00 [INFO] completed JOB-INTEREST
2026-11-01 00:00:00 [INFO] executing JOB-REPORT-1 (report) attempt 1
2026-11-01 00:00:00 [INFO] executing JOB-REPORT-2 (report) attempt 1
2026-11-01 00:00:00 [WARNING] tenant CORP at cap, deferring JOB-REPORT-3
2026-11-01 00:00:00 [INFO] Simulating interest worker crash (lease expires)...
2026-11-01 00:00:00 [WARNING] dedup: effect of JOB-INTEREST already applied, skipping
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  schedule jobs (interest, 4×report, statement) dueAt=now
    │
    ▼
  Scheduler.dispatchDue(now)
    │ store.dueJobs → PENDING & due
    │ claim(job) with lease (PENDING→RUNNING, atomic)
    ▼
  WorkerPool.submit(job)
    │
    ├─ tenant under cap?              ├─ tenant at cap (CORP, 2 running)
    │  execute                        │  defer (RUNNING→PENDING)
    │  dedup check (effect seen?)     │
    │   ├─ no → run + record effect   │
    │   └─ yes → skip (no double)     │
    ▼                                 ▼
  DONE                              retry later

  interest worker CRASH → expireLease → PENDING
    │ re-dispatch
    │ effect already recorded → DEDUP skip
    ▼
  DONE (interest applied exactly once)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Task Scheduler ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Lease/claim (lock): atomic PENDING→RUNNING, re-dispatch  │
  │  At-least-once + dedup: stable effect id → exactly-once   │
  │  Retry with backoff + dead-letter after max attempts      │
  │  Per-tenant fairness: concurrency cap per tenant          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Store persists, Scheduler claims, Pool executes       │
  │  O: new retry policy = swap, scheduler unchanged          │
  │  D: Scheduler + Pool depend on JobStore abstraction       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────┐
  │     Scheduler        │─────▶│       JobStore       │
  │ - store              │ uses │ + schedule/dueJobs   │
  │ + dispatchDue        │      │ + get/expireLease    │
  │ - claim(job,lease)   │      └──────────────────────┘
  └──────────┬───────────┘      ┌──────────────────────┐
             │ submits          │         Job          │
             ▼                  │ - state, attempts    │
      ┌──────────────┐          │ - leaseOwner/expiry  │
      │  WorkerPool  │─────────▶│ + incrementAttempts  │
      │ + submit     │ runs     └──────────────────────┘
      │ - execute    │ dedup set, per-tenant counts
      └──────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Job ─────────────────────────────────────

  [PENDING] ──claim──→ [RUNNING] ──success──→ [DONE]
      ▲                   │
      │ lease expire      │ fail (attempts<max)
      │ / tenant cap      ▼
      └───────────────[PENDING] ──attempts=max──→ [DEAD]

  ── Call Chain (crash + dedup) ─────────────────────────────

  1. scheduler.dispatchDue(now)
  2.   → claim(JOB-INTEREST) PENDING→RUNNING
  3.   → workers.submit → execute → record effect → DONE
  4. store.expireLease(JOB-INTEREST) → RUNNING→PENDING (crash sim)
  5. scheduler.dispatchDue(now+1) → re-claim → execute
  6.   → effect already recorded → DEDUP skip → DONE

  Contract for execute(job):
    Pre:  job claimed with valid lease
    Post: effect applied at most once (dedup by effect id)
    On failure: retry up to MAX_ATTEMPTS then DEAD
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A distributed task scheduler reliably runs jobs at or after a scheduled time across a cluster, and its central challenge is correctness under worker crashes and clock skew. I persist every job durably with its id, due time, payload, tenant, state, and retry bookkeeping, and I index by next-run time so the scheduler can efficiently ask which jobs are due now. Durability is the first requirement because a single cron server is fragile: if it dies, nothing runs, which at National Bank of India once meant daily interest was not applied for a whole night.

The heart of the design is the execution guarantee. I use at-least-once execution, where a worker claims a job with a lease by atomically flipping it from pending to running, so two workers can never run the same job at once, and if a worker crashes the lease expires and the job is re-dispatched. The catch is that at-least-once can run a job twice, for example when a worker completes the work but crashes before acknowledging. So I make the effect idempotent or deduplicated using a stable execution id: the second run recognizes the effect is already applied and skips it. In the interest example, this is what prevents interest from being applied twice when a worker crashes after calculating but before reporting success.

Around this I add retry and fairness. A failed job is re-scheduled after a backoff delay up to a maximum number of attempts, after which it moves to a dead-letter state for investigation rather than retrying forever and masking a real bug. Multi-tenant isolation keeps the system fair: jobs carry a tenant id, and I cap how many jobs a single tenant can run concurrently, so when one corporate customer floods the scheduler with thousands of report jobs, a retail customer like Rajesh still gets his statement job run on time.

The subtle operational point I always raise is tuning the lease and recording completion atomically with releasing it. A lease must be long enough to cover legitimate execution but short enough that a dead worker's job is recovered quickly, and completion must be committed in the same atomic step that releases the lease, otherwise a job could be marked done and still re-dispatched, or re-dispatched and then marked done out of order. Getting the lease, deduplication, retry, and tenant fairness right together is what turns a fragile single cron into a scheduler a bank can trust with its money-moving jobs.
